new_statements.quote: [p.16] The language is tonal with three level tones (high ՛, mid and low ̀). In this article, the high and low tones are marked while the mid tone is unmarked. [...] [p.17] The use of stress to distinguish compounds and phrases as suggested by Booij (2005) and Giegerich (2005) is limited to English and other languages that are intonational. But in tonal languages like Eggon, stress does not exist and cannot distinguish words and phrases. [...] [p.24] This, however, may not apply to some languages that do not make use of stress to distinguish words and phrases such as Eggon. Even though Eggon makes use of tone, it does not distinguish words and phrases.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Eggon is described as a tone language with three level tones (H, M, L; rare contours); the (native-speaker) author asserts that stress does not exist in Eggon and plays no role in distinguishing compounds from phrases. No positive statement of any word-level prominence position exists in any source opened.
new_statements.exceptions: none; the statement is a blanket assertion made in passing within a morphosyntactic study, not the result of a prosodic analysis
new_statements.domain_note: Statement concerns the absence of stress generally and specifically as a compound-vs-phrase diagnostic (word/phrase level). The only dedicated phonological description (Sibomana 1985, Kagbu dialect) was not accessible, and Blench's 2015 dictionary introduction (based on Sibomana) describes tones only and is silent on stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Garba & Dansabo 2026 describe Eggon generally (first author a native speaker, Nasarawa State University Keffi; dialect not specified). Sibomana 1985 (unseen) focuses on the Kagbu dialect; Mwanti & Alagbe 2025 describe the Wana dialect. All are eggo1239; Glottolog lists no sub-dialect codes used here.

sources.note: p.16: Eggon is tonal with three level tones (H, M, L). p.17: 'in tonal languages like Eggon, stress does not exist and cannot distinguish words and phrases.' p.24: Eggon is among languages 'that do not make use of stress to distinguish words and phrases'; tone does not distinguish compounds from phrases either (p.27). Passing remark by a native-speaker linguist, not a phonological analysis.

sources.citation: Mwanti, Rebecca Sunday & Adewole A. Alagbe. 2025. The morphophonemics of tense and aspects in Wana dialect of Eggon language in contrast with English language. Greener Journal of Language and Literature Research 10(1): 1-9. doi:10.15580/gjllr.2025.1.061925105
sources.note: Three contrastive level tones plus contours (citing Blench's dictionary and Timothy 2023 MA thesis); tense is marked by tone on the verb agreement prefix (H future, M non-future). Nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Garba, Patience Ashesla. 2024. Lexical ambiguity in Eggon language. Tropical Journal of Arts and Humanities 6(1): 1-8. doi:10.47524/tjah.v6i1.2
sources.note: p.1: Eggon is tonal; H and L marked, M unmarked; contour tones exist but are rare. Tone disambiguates lexical items. Nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Nkamigbo, Linda Chinelo. 2014. The expression of nominal plurality in Eggon. In: In the Perspectives of Language and Literature: Essays in Honour of R.U. Uzoezie, ch. 13, 154-159.
sources.note: p.158: 'The Eggon language attests three level tones namely: high, mid and low'; tonal permutation marks plural. Nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Maddieson, Ian. 1981. Unusual consonant clusters and complex segments in Eggon. Studies in African Linguistics, Supplement 8 (Précis from the 12th Conference on African Linguistics), 89-92.
sources.note: Consonant clusters and complex segments arising from medial-vowel deletion (CVCV > CCV); nothing on stress or accent.

sources.citation: Blench, Roger (ed.; from a 1940s ms. by I.D. Hepburn, with Ian Maddieson's fieldnotes). 2015. A dictionary of Eggon. Draft printout, 6 January 2015. Cambridge: Kay Williamson Educational Foundation. 85 pp.
sources.note: Intro pp.2-4 (phoneme chart after Sibomana 1985): 'There are three level tones and two glides, rising and falling'; V1-deletion yields CCV stems with the deleted vowel's tone kept as a floating tone. Nothing about stress/accent. States 'The only published description of the Eggon sound-system is in Sibomana (1985)'.
